steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our HCI paper on HaLLMark, a system that records and visualizes how writers use an LLM while writing so AI contributions are transparent. Cover the motivation around LLMs in creative writing, our approach, and what we found with writers.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs in creative writing: fears and the need to embrace them responsibly
2. Problem: attributing AI contributions, ownership, policies
3. Our argument: provenance of writer-AI interaction
4. What we did: policy review, HaLLMark probe
5. Evaluation with creative writers and findings
6. Discussion: other stakeholders, broader impact

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LLMs in creative writing
- LLMs here to stay
- panned esp. in creative writing; doomsayers: impossible to tell writer's original work from LLM text
- fear: flood of poor text; writing recycled/regurgitated from forebears' work -> original thought?
- argued: essential aspect of being human lost if machines do creative writing
- valid concerns, but LLMs = another tool in a long line; harness justly, responsibly, ethically rather than suppress

2. Attribution problem
- critical concern: properly attributing AI contributions
- "ownership tension"; hampers agency and control (cite)
- also needed to conform to AI-assisted writing policies (cite)
- authors have few mechanisms to track accountability re rules/policies

3. Argument: provenance
- capture writer-AI interactions as document evolves (= provenance) + interactive exploration
- -> improves agency, control, ownership of final artifact (short stories, novels, poems)
- prior research: externalizing provenance balances automation and agency in human-AI collaboration (cite)
- provenance also helps policy conformance, transparency to publishers and readers

4. What we did
- reviewed guidelines/policy docs on LLM use: professional, educational, academic orgs (Section 3)
- -> types of info writers should be aware of
- HaLLMark: web-based technology probe (cite); authoring interface + LLM support; stores and visualizes interaction (Section 4)
- helps self-reflection on AI use, clearly highlights AI contributions

5. Evaluation
- creative writers write a short story, remote sessions; feedback + stories (Section 5)
- writers actively evaluate AI assistance from the start
- sense of control, improved ownership
- helps conform to policies without manually generating disclosures
- confident: more transparent; effective medium to communicate AI use to external parties (publishers)

6. Discussion
- other stakeholders: readers, peer-reviewers, publishers (Section 6)
- broader impact: ethical LLM use in writing and publication industry

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are here to stay. Their arrival has been widely panned, especially in creative writing, where doomsayers say that in the future it will be impossible to tell the difference between a writer's original work and text that an LLM generated. Also, people fear that LLMs could flood us with lots of poor text. What happens to original thought if we always read writing that is recycled and regurgitated from original work that was already produced by our forebears? Some have even argued that an essential part of what it means to be human is lost if machines do creative writing. These concerns are valid, but LLMs are still just another tool in a long line of tools, and we should find ways to use the technology in a just, responsible, and ethical way instead of trying to suppress it. But when writers try to embrace this technology, one critical concern for those who want to use LLMs is how to properly attribute the contributions from the AI. This creates an "ownership tension" for writers and hampers their agency and control over the process. Identifying AI contributions is also important for writers who have to conform to AI-assisted writing policies. Right now authors have few mechanisms to track their accountability with respect to these rules and policies.

In this work we argue that capturing the interactions between AI and writers as the document evolves (i.e., provenance information) and supporting interactive exploration of this provenance information will improve the writer's agency, control, and ownership of the final artifact (e.g., short stories, novels, poems). Prior research suggests that externalizing provenance can help balance automation and agency in human-AI collaboration. Provenance can also help writers conform to AI-assisted writing policies and give transparency to publishers and readers. To explore this design space, we first reviewed existing guidelines and policy documents about using LLMs from several professional, educational, and academic organizations (Section 3). This review told us what types of information writers should be aware of in AI-assisted writing. Then we developed HaLLMark, a web-based technology probe that integrates an authoring interface with LLM support and stores and visualizes the writer's interaction with the LLM (Section 4). The system helps writers self-reflect on their AI use by clearly highlighting the AI contributions.

5. Evaluation
- creative writers write a short story, remote sessions; feedback + stories (Section 5)
- writers actively evaluate AI assistance from the start
- sense of control, improved ownership
- helps conform to policies without manually generating disclosures
- confident: more transparent; effective medium to communicate AI use to external parties (publishers)

6. Discussion
- other stakeholders: readers, peer-reviewers, publishers (Section 6)
- broader impact: ethical LLM use in writing and publication industry

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are here to stay. Their arrival has been widely panned, especially in creative writing, where doomsayers say that in the future it will be impossible to tell the difference between a writer's original work and text that an LLM generated. Also, people fear that LLMs could flood us with lots of poor text. What happens to original thought if we always read writing that is recycled and regurgitated from original work that was already produced by our forebears? Some have even argued that an essential part of what it means to be human is lost if machines do creative writing. These concerns are valid, but LLMs are still just another tool in a long line of tools, and we should find ways to use the technology in a just, responsible, and ethical way instead of trying to suppress it. But when writers try to embrace this technology, one critical concern for those who want to use LLMs is how to properly attribute the contributions from the AI. This creates an "ownership tension" for writers and hampers their agency and control over the process. Identifying AI contributions is also important for writers who have to conform to AI-assisted writing policies. Right now authors have few mechanisms to track their accountability with respect to these rules and policies.

In this work we argue that capturing the interactions between AI and writers as the document evolves (i.e., provenance information) and supporting interactive exploration of this provenance information will improve the writer's agency, control, and ownership of the final artifact (e.g., short stories, novels, poems). Prior research suggests that externalizing provenance can help balance automation and agency in human-AI collaboration. Provenance can also help writers conform to AI-assisted writing policies and give transparency to publishers and readers. To explore this design space, we first reviewed existing guidelines and policy documents about using LLMs from several professional, educational, and academic organizations (Section 3). This review told us what types of information writers should be aware of in AI-assisted writing. Then we developed HaLLMark, a web-based technology probe that integrates an authoring interface with LLM support and stores and visualizes the writer's interaction with the LLM (Section 4). The system helps writers self-reflect on their AI use by clearly highlighting the AI contributions.

To validate HaLLMark, we had a group of creative writers use it to write a short story in remote evaluation sessions, and we collected their feedback and the stories they wrote (Section 5). Our findings suggest that HaLLMark encouraged writers to actively evaluate the AI assistance from the start of the writing process. This gave the writers a sense of control and improved their ownership of the final artifact. The findings also suggest that HaLLMark will help writers conform to AI-assisted writing policies without having to manually generate disclosures. So writers were confident that HaLLMark will help them be more transparent and that it is an effective medium for communicating AI use in writing to external parties (i.e., publishers). At the end of the paper we outline how other stakeholders (e.g., readers, peer-reviewers, publishers) could use and benefit from our approach (Section 6). We also discuss the broader impact of our work on the ethical use of LLMs in the writing and publication industry.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are here to stay. Their arrival has been particularly widely panned in creative writing, where doomsayers are hinting at a future in which it will become impossible to distinguish between a writer's original work and text generated by an LLM. Worse, LLMs are feared to potentially inundate us with a cornucopia of poor text. What happens to original thought if we are subjected to writing forever recycled and regurgitated from original work already produced by our forebears? It has even been argued that some essential aspect of what it means to be human is lost if creative writing is performed by machines. While these are valid concerns, LLMs are just another tool in a long line of tools, and we should find ways to harness the technology in a just, responsible, and ethical way rather than attempt to suppress it. But in trying to embrace this technology, one critical concern for writers who want to use LLMs is properly attributing contributions from the AI. This gives rise to an "ownership tension" among writers and hampers their agency and control over the process [1,2]. Identifying contributions from AI is also important for writers who need to conform to AI-assisted writing policies [3,4]. Authors currently have few mechanisms to track their accountability with regard to these rules and policies.

In this work, we argue that capturing interactions between AI and writers as the document evolves (i.e., provenance information) and supporting interactive exploration of such provenance information will improve the writer's agency, control, and ownership of the final artifact (e.g., short stories, novels, poems). Prior research suggests that externalizing provenance can help balance automation and agency in human-AI collaboration [5]. Provenance can also help writers conform to AI-assisted writing policies and provide transparency to publishers and readers. To explore this design space, we first reviewed existing guidelines and policy documents on the use of LLMs from several professional, educational, and academic organizations (Section 3). This review informed us about the types of information writers should be aware of in AI-assisted writing. We then developed HaLLMark, a web-based technology probe [6] that integrates an authoring interface with LLM support and stores and visualizes a writer's interaction with an LLM (Section 4). The system helps writers self-reflect on their use of AI by clearly highlighting AI contributions.

To validate HaLLMark, we engaged a group of creative writers to use it to write a short story during remote evaluation sessions and collected their feedback and resulting stories (Section 5). Our findings suggest HaLLMark encouraged writers to actively evaluate AI assistance from the onset of the writing process. As a result, it instilled a sense of control and improved ownership of the final artifact. Our findings also suggest HaLLMark will help writers conform to AI-assisted writing policies without the need to manually generate disclosures. Writers were therefore confident that HaLLMark will help them become more transparent and that it is an effective medium for communicating the use of AI in writing to external parties (i.e., publishers). We close the paper by outlining how other stakeholders (e.g., readers, peer-reviewers, publishers) could use and benefit from our approach (Section 6). We also discuss the broader impact of our work on the ethical use of LLMs in the writing and publication industry.
